clue.text: What makes bio big and worthless?

parts.note: the words bio and big differ in one letter: G (good) stands where O (nothing, zero) stood, which is what the answer read as an instruction says

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about turning biology into something large, tacked onto a sneer at worthlessness.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: G is the abbreviation for good and O looks like zero, so 'good for nothing' read literally means swap G in for O, which is what changes bio to big.
explanation.definitionFit: A layabout of no use to anyone is described by this phrase, a common idiom for being of no value.

clue.text: Desperately we ask — no, beg — Charlie not to retaliate

indicators.note: acting desperately suggests wild, disordered behaviour, so the letters that follow are thrown into a new order

parts.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone pleads desperately with Charlie not to take revenge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Desperately' signals an anagram of WE ASK, NO, BEG, C and NOT together; the dashes are just punctuation for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To pay someone back for a wrong done to you is an idiom for taking revenge, i.e. retaliating.

clue.text: Belted hunter scoffing at speech

indicators.note: to scoff is to eat greedily, so the hunter takes the next word into his middle

parts.note: Orion, the constellation of the hunter, is famous for its belt of three stars

explanation.surface: A hunter wearing a belt mocks a speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scoffing' looks like mocking, but it means gobbling up.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal address delivered to an audience is a speech, often a grand or ceremonial one.

clue.text: Fling is overlooked by female, I suspect

indicators.note: in a down clue, a piece overlooked by others sits beneath them, so the fling word comes after the female and the I

parts.note: to fling is to throw, and to shy is to throw too, as at a coconut shy

explanation.surface: Someone suspects a woman is turning a blind eye to an affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fling' looks like an affair, but it is a throw, SHY. 'I suspect' seems to be the speaker's aside; 'suspect' is actually the definition, used as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that arouses doubt or seems dodgy is suspect, and fishy is the colloquial word for that.

clue.text: Centre of Paris sadly has good and bad drivers

indicators.note: the centre of a five-letter word is its third letter, here taken from Paris
something going sadly goes wrong, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Central Paris, unfortunately, has both good and bad motorists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'good and' reads as a contrast with 'bad drivers', but 'has good' is the anagram fodder after 'sadly'.
explanation.definitionFit: Motorists who drive selfishly, hogging the lane, are given this scornful name.

clue.text: Evidently short of time too

indicators.note: being short of something means lacking it, so the time letter is dropped

parts.note: something done evidently is done openly, i.e. overtly

explanation.surface: Plainly lacking time as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'too' looks like 'as well' but means excessively.
explanation.definitionFit: Too as in 'too keen' means excessively, which is the sense of the adverb here.

clue.text: He explored two British writers

parts.note: two British writers are named: the first, Georgette Heyer, was the Regency romance novelist
the second writer is Roald Dahl, the British children's author

explanation.surface: A man investigated a pair of British authors.
explanation.walkthrough: The two writers' surnames are joined. Thor Heyerdahl was the Norwegian explorer who sailed the raft Kon-Tiki across the Pacific.
explanation.definitionFit: Thor Heyerdahl made famous expeditions by raft and reed boat, so he is a man who explored.

clue.text: Series about entertaining English individual displaying a bit of nerve

indicators.note: to entertain is to host a guest, so the reversed word holds the English letter inside
about here means turned round, so the series word is written backwards

parts.note: a run is a series, as a run of wins
one means a single individual

explanation.surface: A TV series featuring an English loner showing courage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a bit of nerve' sounds like courage, but it is literally part of the nervous system.
explanation.definitionFit: A nerve cell is a basic unit of the nervous system, so it is a bit of a nerve; this is the older spelling.

clue.text: Gent almost picked up prize in game — a piece of furniture

indicators.note: in means the gent and prize pieces sit within the game word

parts.note: chess is a board game

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the gent word loses its last letter

parts.note: a toff is an upper-class gentleman

indicators.note: in a down clue, picking up lifts the word so it reads from bottom to top, i.e. backwards

parts.note: a reward is a prize

explanation.surface: A gentleman nearly collected a prize during a game, then a stray mention of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' places the shortened gent and the reversed prize together inside the game, splitting its last letter off from the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A bedroom cabinet with sliding compartments for clothes is a common item of furniture.

clue.text: Possibly start with Latin, changing it back to English?

definitions.text: Possibly start with Latin, changing it back to English?

indicators.note: possibly signals that the letters could be arranged in another way, an anagram
changing one thing to another means swapping letters, here the reversed it for English
back means the word it is read in reverse

explanation.surface: A suggestion to begin with a Latin text and render it in English.
explanation.walkthrough: In STARTLATIN, swap TI ('it back') for E, 'changing' it to English; that gives STARTLAEN, and 'Possibly' rearranges it. The whole clue also describes the act.
explanation.definitionFit: Rendering a Latin passage into English is what a classics student does when converting text between languages.

clue.text: Teenager's not entirely happy out here

indicators.note: not entirely means only part of the phrase is used, so the letters sit within these words

explanation.surface: A teenager is only partly content out here.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is' linking the definition to the wordplay; the letters run across happY OUT Here.
explanation.definitionFit: A young person in their teens is a youth, a common synonym for adolescent.

clue.text: One stops interfering, becoming vociferous

indicators.note: a stopper plugs a gap, so one goes into the middle of the interfering word

parts.note: nosy describes someone prying into others' affairs
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone stops meddling and starts shouting instead.
explanation.definitionFit: A vociferous crowd is loud and clamorous, so the two words share the sense of making a lot of noise.

clue.text: Shifting hair oil, American makes killing

indicators.note: shifting means moving about, so the letters of the hair product are rearranged

parts.note: US stands for United States, so it can mean American

explanation.surface: An American makes a fortune selling hair oil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'makes killing' suggests a big profit, but 'killing' is the definition in its sense of extremely funny; 'makes' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A killing joke or performance is extremely funny, an informal sense of the word meaning side-splitting.

clue.text: City's playing against Lazio for final

indicators.note: playing suggests moving around freely, so the letters of the word are jumbled
final points to the last letter of the Italian club's name

explanation.surface: Manchester City face Lazio in a cup final.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is' linking definition to wordplay; 'for' links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Santiago is the capital of Chile, so it is a city; the name is shared by Santiago de Compostela in Spain.

clue.text: Popular setter secures right to get pay rise

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast, so the setter word holds the right letter inside

parts.note: cement is something that sets hard

explanation.surface: A well-liked crossword setter wins a raise in salary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'setter' invites a crossword compiler, but it is something that sets.
explanation.definitionFit: An increment is a regular step up in salary, so it is an addition to one's wages.

clue.text: Look round, taking in baron's summerhouse

indicators.note: taking in means admitting something inside, so the baron letter goes into the other letters

parts.note: to gaze is to look steadily
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Someone looks about, visiting a nobleman's garden pavilion.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's after baron is a link; B goes between GAZE and O.
explanation.definitionFit: A gazebo is a garden pavilion with a view, the same kind of small open garden building.

clue.text: Old English houses start to captivate member of church

indicators.note: to house something is to hold it within, so the old English word holds the first letter of captivate

parts.note: Anglian refers to the Angles, early settlers whose dialects formed Old English

indicators.note: the start to a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Old English homes begin to win people over to the church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'houses' looks like a noun but is the verb holding the C inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A follower of the Church of England is known by this name, so they are a member of that church.

clue.text: We're told gag, an unfortunate sort

indicators.note: something we are told is something heard, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: to gag is to heave as if about to vomit, i.e. to retch

explanation.surface: A sad character told a joke, so we hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gag' looks like a joke but is the throat's heave.
explanation.definitionFit: A miserable or pitiable person, someone luckless or downtrodden, is called this.

clue.text: Summary of largely impressive book

indicators.note: largely means for the most part, so the impressive word loses its last letter

parts.note: epic means grand or impressive
a tome is a large book

explanation.surface: An outline of a mostly impressive book.
explanation.definitionFit: An epitome is a condensed abstract of a work, so it means a précis or digest; it now usually means a perfect example.

clue.text: At home, renowned boxing legend initially gets angry

parts.note: in means at home, as in staying in

indicators.note: boxing means putting in a box, so the renowned word encloses the first letter of legend

parts.note: famed means renowned

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A famous boxer, home for once, loses his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boxing legend' reads as a famous fighter, but 'boxing' encloses the L and 'gets' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflamed passions are heated, so someone inflamed is enraged or furious.

clue.text: A disfigurement concealed by Mum's cosmetic

indicators.note: something concealed by another is hidden within it, so the A and disfigurement go inside the mother word

parts.note: Ma is an informal word for Mum; the possessive belongs to the surface
a scar is a disfiguring mark

explanation.surface: Mum's make-up covers a blemish.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the make-up covers a blemish; in the wordplay it is Mum who does the concealing.
explanation.definitionFit: Mascara is make-up applied to the eyelashes, so it is a cosmetic product.

clue.text: Chuck Norris's heading for paradise

parts.note: to chuck is to throw, i.e. heave

indicators.note: a heading comes at the top, so the first letter of the name is taken

explanation.surface: The actor Chuck Norris is on his way to paradise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chuck Norris' reads as the martial-arts film star, but 'Chuck' is the verb meaning throw.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise is the abode of the blessed after death, the same idea as the afterlife's bliss.

clue.text: Nick's encouraging report on newly-wed's health?

parts.note: a bride is a newly-wed woman
saying someone is well is good news about their health, the word that ends the clue

explanation.surface: Good news on how a new spouse is faring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' is slang for prison. Bridewell was a famous old London prison, and its name became a general word for a jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Nick is British slang for a prison or police station, and this old word likewise means a house of correction.

clue.text: Tenor's given award, mostly for opera

parts.note: T is an abbreviation for tenor; the 's is the surface's possessive

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all, so the award loses its last letter

parts.note: an Oscar is a film award

explanation.surface: A tenor is handed an award for an opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosca is Puccini's opera about the singer Floria Tosca, so it is one particular opera.

clue.text: Charges pound to block opening up

indicators.note: to block an opening is to fill it, so the pound letter goes inside
in a down clue, up means the word reads from bottom to top, i.e. backwards

parts.note: a slot is an opening
L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Fees, a pound coin jammed in a slot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening up' looks like unlocking, but 'up' reverses SLOT, and L goes into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolls are fees paid for using a road or bridge, so they are charges.

clue.text: Part of bulb cracked

definitions.meaning: a segment of a bulb of garlic
the past tense of cleave, to split

explanation.walkthrough: 'cracked' looks like an adjective meaning broken, but it is the old past tense of cleave.
explanation.definitionFit: A segment of a garlic bulb has this name, and the same word is the old past tense of cleave, to split.

clue.text: Unfortunate, having to quit holding sway

indicators.note: holding means keeping something inside, so the quitting word wraps the unfortunate word

parts.note: to vacate a place is to quit it
ill means unlucky, as in ill fortune

explanation.surface: Sadly forced to leave while still in power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'holding sway' reads as having power, but 'sway' is the definition, the verb waver.
explanation.definitionFit: To sway between options is to waver indecisively, so the two words share the sense of wavering.

clue.text: Renovation of store's no reason to take it easy

indicators.note: renovating something rebuilds it in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Refurbishing the shop is no excuse for slacking off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Renovation of' signals an anagram of STORE'S NO REASON; 'to' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Rowers who stop pulling and let the boat drift give this idiom for relaxing after effort.
